narrative:
The model estimates a 47% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three main factors shaped this outlook. First, your total years of experience across all jobs stands out as the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward staying. With only 1-5 years overall, you fall into the most common group among employees the model expects to remain, yet the system sees shorter overall experience as a stabilizing signal rather than a risk.

The second strongest driver works in the opposite direction: having received other job offers while at your current employer pulls the prediction toward leaving. This suggests the model interprets external opportunities as a sign you may be considering alternatives.

Third, the limited number of training programs you attended in the past three years also nudges the outcome toward leaving. Most employees predicted to stay have either none or a similar low count, but in your case the model reads this as reduced connection to the organization.

Taken together, your solid emotional commitment, recognition from managers, and sense of job stability are encouraging, yet the combination of outside offers and modest training involvement outweighs them enough to raise concern.

The organization should discuss retention steps with you, such as clearer promotion paths or additional development opportunities. You may want to reflect on whether those external offers better match your long-term goals. Addressing these points openly could change the outlook for both sides. (248 words)
